newsitem.title: UK: Despite Dunblane, Britain not gun-crazy society.
newsitem.headline: Despite Dunblane, Britain not gun-crazy society.

text.p: The horrific killing of 16 infants and their teacher in Dunblane, Scotland, in March revealed how easily guns could be obtained legally in Britain.
But Britain is by the standards of many developed countries not a society in thrall to the gun.
Its police have long been famous for walking the streets armed with nothing more than a truncheon for protection.
Violent deaths involving firearms totalled just 75 in England, Wales and Scotland in 1994, down from 82 in 1993, in a population of 56.7 million.

Incidents involving violent injury caused by guns totalled 1,086 in 1994. There were 5,409 incidents where guns were used but not fired. Britons found in possession of illegal firearms face sentences of up to 10 years in prison and heavy fines.
Rules for the granting of certificates were laid down in the 1968 Firearms Act and the 1988 Firearms (Amendments) Act.
ThIs was passed after Michael Ryan shot dead 16 people, including his own mother, in the southern English town of Hungerford in 1987. Ryan held licences for his guns.

The 1988 act prohibits people who have been jailed for more than three years from having a certificate. Britons who have been jailed for between three months and three years are entitled to apply for a certificate after a wait of five years.
Controls on possession of guns have existed since 1820. Possession of pistols, revolvers and rifles has required a police certificate since 1920.

Machineguns have been prohibited since 1937 and all shotguns have needed a licence since 1967. The 1988 act banned self-loading rifles and semi-automatic shotguns. As well as undertaking to keep their arms in a secure place, applicants must show they are not a danger to the public and show they will have "regular and legitimate opportunity for using the weapon".

In practice, this will often mean they must be members of one of the country's 2,118 approved gun clubs. Thomas Hamilton, the loner who used four handguns in the Dunblane massacre, held firearms licences and was a member of a local gun club.
According to a recent parliamentary report, there were 174,020 firearms certificates on issue, plus 722,620 shot gun certificates, in 1995.
Some 57,000 of the certificates permitted the holding of handguns, and there were over 200,000 guns held on these certificates, the Home Affairs Committee report said.
Only around one percent of licence applications are turned down.
About 10 percent of handguns are 0.22 inch calibre, used in Olympic and international target shooting competition.

The police are reluctant to estimate the number of illegally held guns. But Sir Jim Sharples, president of the Association of Chief Police Officers, told the committee estimates varied from 200,000 to one million.
At the time of the Dunblane massacres, media reports put the number of illegal guns in Britain at up to three million.

An amnesty announced after the massacre yielded 22,939 guns and 695,197 rounds of ammunition. A similar amnesty after the Hungerford incident saw 48,000 weapons handed in together with 1.5 million rounds of ammunition.
